title: SPDX license identifiers
description: SPDX identifiers are the standard short names for licenses — MIT, Apache-2.0, GPL-3.0-only — maintained by the Linux Foundation. Every package should declare one in its metadata; auditors match identifiers instead of parsing license text. The expression syntax handles combos: (MIT OR Apache-2.0), GPL-2.0-only WITH Classpath-exception. No identifier, no automation — that is the rule to enforce first.
mechanism: Match package metadata license fields against the SPDX list; expressions parsed with AND/OR/WITH. Flag unknown/nonstandard identifiers for manual review.
algo: O(packages) matching. The list is curated; expressions are parsed, not regexed.

title: Copyleft detection
description: Copyleft licenses (GPL, AGPL) require derivative works to share source — the clause that keeps lawyers up at night. Detection scans dependencies for copyleft identifiers and, critically, checks linkage: static linking to GPL code generally triggers copyleft; the AGPL triggers on network use. The analysis maps which copyleft code touches which product boundary.
mechanism: Flag copyleft-licensed deps; analyze linkage (static/dynamic/modified); check distribution model (shipped vs SaaS — AGPL matters for SaaS). Report per product, not per repo.
algo: O(deps) flagging + linkage analysis. The legal interpretation is human; the inventory is automated.
demo:
COPYLEFT = {'GPL-3.0-only', 'GPL-2.0-only', 'AGPL-3.0-only'}
deps = [
    ('lib-a', 'MIT', 'dynamic'),
    ('lib-b', 'GPL-3.0-only', 'static'),
    ('lib-c', 'AGPL-3.0-only', 'saas-use'),
]
for name, lic, how in deps:
    flag = lic in COPYLEFT
    print('%-8s %-14s %-10s %s' % (name, lic, how,
          'COPYLEFT: review linkage/distribution!' if flag else 'ok'))
print('static GPL link and AGPL SaaS use are the cases that need lawyers')

title: License compatibility matrix
description: Not all licenses mix: GPL-2.0-only code cannot combine with Apache-2.0 code in one work (the famous incompatibility), while MIT mixes with everything. The compatibility matrix answers 'can I combine A and B?' — and the answer depends on direction (permissive into copyleft is fine; copyleft into permissive is not). Auditors check the transitive closure, not just direct deps.
mechanism: Matrix of (A, B) -> compatible/incompatible/needs-review. Compute over the full dependency graph; the project's license must be compatible with every dep's requirements. Flag one-way incompatibilities with direction.
algo: O(deps^2) pairwise in the worst case; in practice O(deps) against the project license + copyleft checks.
demo:
# simplified compatibility: can project license P include dep license D?
COMPAT = {
    ('MIT', 'MIT'): True, ('MIT', 'Apache-2.0'): True, ('MIT', 'GPL-3.0-only'): True,
    ('Apache-2.0', 'MIT'): True, ('Apache-2.0', 'GPL-2.0-only'): False,  # famous incompatibility
    ('GPL-3.0-only', 'MIT'): True, ('GPL-3.0-only', 'Apache-2.0'): True,
}
project, deps = 'Apache-2.0', ['MIT', 'GPL-2.0-only', 'BSD-3-Clause']
for d in deps:
    ok = COMPAT.get((project, d), 'review')
    print('project %s + dep %s: %s' % (project, d, ok))
print('direction matters: permissive INTO copyleft is fine; reverse is not')

title: SBOM generation
description: A Software Bill of Materials lists every component in the shipped product — name, version, license, supplier, hash — in CycloneDX or SPDX format. Governments now require SBOMs for sold software (US Executive Order 14028); auditors consume them automatically. Generation hooks into the build: lockfiles in, SBOM out, attached to every release artifact.
mechanism: Parse lockfiles/manifests; resolve licenses; emit CycloneDX JSON; sign and attach to the release. Regenerate per build — SBOMs rot fast.
algo: O(deps) per build. The SBOM is only as good as the lockfile — unpinned deps produce fiction.

title: Dependency scanning
description: Dependency scanning inventories every third-party component — direct and transitive — and checks each against license policies and vulnerability databases. The transitive part is what surprises teams: the average project has 10x more transitive deps than direct ones. Scanners resolve the full graph from lockfiles and report per product, per release.
mechanism: Resolve lockfile -> full graph; enrich with license + vuln data; evaluate policy; report. Run on every build; diff against the last release to show what changed.
algo: O(deps) graph walk. Transitives dominate — direct deps are the tip.

title: Attribution requirements
description: Permissive licenses are not public domain — MIT, BSD, and Apache-2.0 all require attribution (keep the copyright notice), and Apache-2.0 additionally requires documenting changes. Attribution automation collects NOTICES from every dep and bundles them into the product's legal screen or NOTICE file. Missing attribution is the most common license violation, and the easiest to fix automatically.
mechanism: Collect license texts + copyright lines per dep; render into NOTICE; include in distributions (app legal screen, docs). Apache-2.0: append change log entries.
algo: O(deps) collection. Automate it — manual attribution rots on the first dep update.
demo:
deps = [
    ('requests', 'Copyright (c) Kenneth Reitz', 'Apache-2.0'),
    ('click', 'Copyright (c) Armin Ronacher', 'BSD-3-Clause'),
]
notice = ['THIRD-PARTY NOTICES', '']
for name, copy, lic in deps:
    notice += ['%s (%s)' % (name, lic), copy, '']
print('\n'.join(notice))
print('bundled into the product automatically, every release')

title: Policy engines
description: Policy engines turn legal guidance into executable rules: 'deny GPL in shipped products', 'allow MIT everywhere', 'review required for unknown licenses'. Policies are code (Rego, YAML), versioned with the repo, and evaluated on every build. The engine's output is allow/deny/review per component with the rule cited — auditability built in.
mechanism: Policy as code; evaluate component list against rules; verdicts with rule references. Exceptions are explicit waivers with expiry, not silent skips.
algo: O(deps * rules). Waivers expire — no permanent silent exceptions.

title: CI gates for licenses
description: License gates in CI fail the build on policy violations — a new GPL dependency cannot merge without review. The gate diffs the dependency set against the base branch, so only new deps are judged (grandfathering existing ones with a ratchet). Findings post as PR comments with the license, the policy rule, and the waiver process. Three minutes, every PR, no exceptions.
mechanism: On PR: resolve deps, diff vs base, evaluate policy on new deps, fail on deny/review-needed. Waivers via annotated config with expiry. Nightly full scans catch policy changes affecting old deps.
algo: O(new deps) per PR. The ratchet keeps it about new code.

title: Dual licensing
description: Dual-licensed projects offer a choice — GPL for open source users, commercial license for everyone else (MySQL's model) — or permissive-or-copyleft options. Auditors must record which license was chosen: the obligations follow the choice, not the options. Detection reads the project's declared options plus the consumer's selection file; 'we use the commercial license' needs to be on record, not assumed.
mechanism: Record per-dep the chosen license from the declared options; obligations computed from the choice. Commercial license receipts stored with the SBOM.
algo: O(deps) bookkeeping. The choice must be explicit and recorded.
demo:
OPTIONS = {'db-lib': ['GPL-3.0-only', 'Commercial-1.0']}
chosen = {'db-lib': 'Commercial-1.0'}  # on record, with receipt

for dep, opts in OPTIONS.items():
    c = chosen.get(dep)
    print('%s options: %s' % (dep, opts))
    print('  chosen: %s %s' % (c, '(obligations follow the CHOICE)' if c else '(UNRECORDED: assumed GPL!)'))
print('unrecorded choice = worst-case obligations assumed')

title: Vendored code auditing
description: Vendored code — third-party source copied into the repo — bypasses package metadata entirely: no version, no license field, just files. Auditing finds it by fingerprinting (hash known releases, match snippets) and treats each vendored copy as a pinned dependency with its license obligations. The policy question is whether vendoring is allowed at all; the audit makes the invisible visible.
mechanism: Hash files/directories against known release fingerprints; snippet-match unknowns; record (path, project, version, license). CI flags new vendored code for review.
algo: O(files) hashing; matching against the fingerprint DB.

title: Binary scanning
description: Sometimes there is no source — acquired products, legacy binaries, container images. Binary scanners identify embedded open-source components from strings, symbols, and code fingerprints inside the binary. It is approximate (version identification is fuzzy), but it finds the GPL library inside the black-box appliance that the vendor 'forgot' to disclose.
mechanism: Extract strings/symbols; match against component signature DB; report candidates with confidence. Container scanning layers this per image layer.
algo: O(binary size) extraction + signature matching. Confidence-scored, human-verified.
demo:
# strings-based component identification inside a 'binary'
binary = b'\x7fELF...libssl.so.1.1...Copyright OpenSSL...GPL-licensed helper...'
SIGNATURES = [(b'OpenSSL', 'openssl', 'Apache-2.0'), (b'GPL-licensed', 'unknown-gpl', 'GPL-?')]

found = [(name, lic) for sig, name, lic in SIGNATURES if sig in binary]
print('components found in binary:')
for name, lic in found:
    print('  %-12s %s' % (name, lic))
print('approximate (fuzzy versions) but finds the undisclosed GPL in the appliance')

title: License remediation
description: When the audit finds a violation, remediation options rank by cost: replace the dep (best), relicense your usage (negotiate commercial), isolate the component (process boundary can change copyleft analysis — consult counsel), or remove the feature. The remediation tracker records the decision, owner, and deadline per finding — violations are bugs with SLAs, not background noise.
mechanism: Finding -> options analysis -> decision recorded -> owner + deadline -> verify (rescan). Track like security vulnerabilities: SLA by severity.
algo: O(findings) tracking. The work is engineering + legal, not algorithmic.
demo:
findings = [
    {'dep': 'gpl-lib', 'issue': 'GPL in shipped product', 'options': ['replace', 'relicense', 'isolate']}]
for f in findings:
    print('finding: %(dep)s: %(issue)s' % f)
    print('  options:', f['options'], '(ranked by cost)')
    print('  decision: REPLACE with mit-alt | owner: eng | due: 30d | verify: rescan')
print('violations are bugs with SLAs, not background noise')

title: Legal review workflows
description: Not every finding needs a lawyer — the workflow triages: automated allow/deny for the clear cases, legal review queue for the ambiguous (unknown licenses, dual-license choices, copyleft edge cases). SLAs keep the queue moving (48h for blocking reviews); the queue's decisions feed back into policy (today's review becomes tomorrow's rule). The goal is lawyers on the hard 5%, automation on the 95%.
mechanism: Triage: policy decides 95%; queue for the rest with context (dep, usage, options); SLA tracking; decisions codified into policy. Metrics: queue depth, time-to-decision.
algo: O(queue) workflow. The feedback loop (review -> policy) is the compounding value.

title: License reports
description: License reports are the audit's product: per-release component lists with licenses, policy verdicts, and waiver status — consumed by legal, customers (SBOM), and procurement. Generation is automatic from the scan data; the report is versioned with the release and retained for the product's lifetime. When a customer asks 'what open source is in this?', the answer is a link, not a project.
mechanism: Scan data -> report templates (legal summary, customer SBOM, procurement risk) -> versioned artifacts. Retention matches the product's support lifetime.
algo: O(deps) rendering. The value is readiness — the answer exists before it is asked.
demo:
deps = [('requests', 'Apache-2.0', 'allow'), ('new-lib', 'GPL-3.0-only', 'DENY'), ('click', 'BSD-3-Clause', 'allow')]
print('LICENSE REPORT -- release 2.4.1')
print('%-12s %-14s %s' % ('component', 'license', 'verdict'))
for n, lic, v in deps:
    print('%-12s %-14s %s' % (n, lic, v))
print('denied: 1 | waived: 0 | retained for product lifetime')
print('customer asks "what OSS is in this?" -> send the link, not a project')

title: Continuous license monitoring
description: Licenses change — projects relicense (the SSPL/BSL wave), deps update, new transitive deps appear. Continuous monitoring watches the dependency graph over time and alerts on license changes, not just violations: 'lib-x changed MIT -> SSPL in 2.0'. The monitor diffs every resolved graph against the last, because the audit is a process, not an event.
mechanism: Per-build graph snapshot; diff licenses vs previous; alert on changes and new copyleft. Track license-change history per dep — the trend informs replacement decisions.
algo: O(deps) diff per build. The alert is on change, catching drift before it becomes violation.
